content: Open book management is a system in which every employee, regardless of their position within the company—from top-level managers to the most junior worker on the factory floor—is regularly guided through the detailed financial statements of the organization. This approach ensures that all employees have a clear understanding of the company’s financial health and performance. The term open book management was coined in 1999. In practical applications, open book management is often accompanied by the implementation of profit-sharing, gain-sharing, or productivity bonuses. This system was first introduced by John Stack at the Springfield Remanufacturing Center Corporation in 1983. Open book management is also considered a component of the corporate democracy model employed by Semco. A related concept is Complexity Leadership Theory, also known as Complex Systems Leadership Theory, which was proposed in 2006. This theory emphasizes the importance of information sharing within organizations. Based on this framework, Hazy has outlined leadership skills that align with those proposed by Anderson and McDaniel. These skills include: Generative leadership Administrative leadership Community-building leadership Information gathering Information utilization Open book management aligns closely with the principle of information sharing, which has been identified as a critical factor in fostering the success and well-being of workforces.
